# Posterior Prediction and Model Checking {#sec-prediction}

```{r}
#| include: false
source("_common.R")
```

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Learning objectives

After this chapter you should be able to:

1. derive and simulate posterior predictive distributions, and decompose predictive uncertainty into its sources;
2. design posterior predictive checks with test quantities and realised discrepancies aimed at specific model assumptions;
3. compute and interpret posterior predictive p-values, and explain why they are not uniformly distributed under the model;
4. analyse Bayesian residuals and recognise common forms of misspecification;
5. evaluate predictive calibration with the probability integral transform, and predictive accuracy with proper scoring rules (log score, CRPS);
6. state the limitations of posterior predictive checking, including double use of the data.
:::

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## Prerequisites

@sec-bayes-paradigm (posterior predictive distribution), @sec-conjugate (Gamma–Poisson), @sec-priors (prior predictive checks), and the law of total variance (@thm-total-variance).
:::

## Motivation {#sec-pred-motivation}

Bayes' theorem tells us how to update beliefs *within* a model. It says nothing about whether the model is any good. A posterior can be precise and wrong: the conjugate Poisson analysis of the insect counts in @sec-conj-insects produced narrow intervals while the sample variances suggested that the Poisson assumption failed. Prediction gives the model a way to be tested. If a model is adequate, data simulated from it should look like the data we observed, at least in the respects we care about. This idea goes back to @box1980sampling and @rubin1984bayesianly, and in its modern form posterior predictive checking is a central part of the Bayesian workflow [@gelman1996posterior; @gelman2013bda, Chapter 6; @gabry2019visualization].

## Definitions and notation {#sec-pred-definitions}

::: {#def-posterior-predictive}
## Posterior predictive distribution and replicated data
For a model with conditionally independent observations, the **posterior predictive distribution** of new data $\tilde y$ is
$$
p(\tilde y\mid y)=\int p(\tilde y\mid\theta)\,\pi(\theta\mid y)\,d\theta.
$$ {#eq-post-pred}
**Replicated data** $y^{\text{rep}}$ are data that could have been observed *in the same experiment* (same design, covariates and sample size) if it were repeated with the same $\theta$. Their posterior predictive distribution is @eq-post-pred with $\tilde y=y^{\text{rep}}$.
:::

::: {#def-test-quantity}
## Test quantities, discrepancies and posterior predictive p-values
A **test quantity** $T(y)$ is a scalar summary of the data, and a **discrepancy** $T(y,\theta)$ may also depend on parameters. The **posterior predictive p-value** (ppp-value) is
$$
p_B=\mathbb P\big(T(y^{\text{rep}},\theta)\ge T(y,\theta)\ \big|\ y\big),
$$ {#eq-ppp}
where the probability is over the joint posterior distribution of $(\theta,y^{\text{rep}})$ [@meng1994posterior; @gelman1996posterior].
:::

The simulation recipe is direct. For each posterior draw $\theta^{(s)}$, draw $y^{\text{rep}(s)}\sim p(\cdot\mid\theta^{(s)})$ and compare $T(y^{\text{rep}(s)},\theta^{(s)})$ with $T(y,\theta^{(s)})$. The proportion of draws in which the replicate is at least as extreme estimates $p_B$.

## Mathematical development {#sec-pred-development}

### Predictive uncertainty {#sec-pred-uncertainty}

By the laws of total expectation and variance (@thm-tower, @thm-total-variance) applied conditionally on $y$,
$$
\mathbb E[\tilde y\mid y]=\mathbb E\big[\mathbb E(\tilde y\mid\theta)\mid y\big],\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(\tilde y\mid y)=\underbrace{\mathbb E\big[\operatorname{Var}(\tilde y\mid\theta)\mid y\big]}_{\text{sampling (aleatoric) variability}}+\underbrace{\operatorname{Var}\big[\mathbb E(\tilde y\mid\theta)\mid y\big]}_{\text{parameter (epistemic) uncertainty}}.
$$ {#eq-pred-variance}
As data accumulate, the second term typically shrinks like $1/n$, while the first does not. A predictive interval therefore never shrinks to zero width, unlike an interval for $\theta$. "Plug-in" predictions that substitute a point estimate $\hat\theta$ for $\theta$ ignore the second term and are overconfident, especially in small samples.

### Posterior predictive checks {#sec-pred-ppc}

A posterior predictive check asks whether the observed data are typical of replicated data with respect to a chosen test quantity. The art is in choosing $T$:

- **Aim $T$ at an assumption that might fail.** For Poisson counts, the variance-to-mean ratio tests overdispersion and the number of zeros tests zero inflation. For time-ordered data, the lag-1 autocorrelation tests independence. For regression models, residual patterns against covariates test the mean structure.
- **Avoid $T$ that the model fits by construction.** For a Poisson model with a free rate, the sample mean is almost perfectly reproduced in every replicate. Its ppp-value will be near $\tfrac12$ whatever the truth, so it tests nothing.
- **Look at graphs, not only numbers.** Overlaying replicated histograms or time series on the observed ones often reveals unanticipated failures [@gabry2019visualization].

A ppp-value near 0 or 1 indicates that the observed data are extreme relative to the model *in the direction measured by T*. It is a measure of discrepancy, not a probability that the model is true.

### Properties of posterior predictive p-values {#sec-pred-ppp-properties}

Classical p-values are uniformly distributed under the null hypothesis. Posterior predictive p-values are not, because the data are used twice: once to fit the model, once to check it.

::: {#prp-ppp-mean}
## ppp-values average one half under the model
Suppose $\theta\sim\pi$, and $y$ and $y^{\text{rep}}$ are conditionally independent given $\theta$ with the same distribution. If $T$ depends on the data only and $T(y)$ has a continuous distribution, then $\mathbb E[p_B(y)]=\tfrac12$, where the expectation is over the prior predictive distribution of $y$.
:::

::: {.proof}
By @thm-tower, $\mathbb E[p_B(y)]=\mathbb E\big[\mathbb P(T(y^{\text{rep}})\ge T(y)\mid y)\big]=\mathbb P\big(T(y^{\text{rep}})\ge T(y)\big)$ under the joint distribution of $(\theta,y,y^{\text{rep}})$. In that joint distribution $(y,y^{\text{rep}})$ is exchangeable: both are drawn independently from $p(\cdot\mid\theta)$ given the same $\theta$. Hence $\mathbb P(T(y^{\text{rep}})\ge T(y))=\mathbb P(T(y)\ge T(y^{\text{rep}}))$. The two events cover the whole space and overlap only on $\{T(y)=T(y^{\text{rep}})\}$, which has probability zero by continuity, so each has probability $\tfrac12$.
:::

The mean is that of a uniform distribution, but the *spread* is generally smaller. When $T$ is closely tied to the fitted parameters, $p_B$ is pulled towards $\frac12$, and @meng1994posterior shows that under the model $\mathbb P(p_B\le\alpha)\le2\alpha$ for such checks: ppp-values are **conservative**. Consequences: a moderate ppp-value (say 0.3) is weak evidence of good fit, an extreme ppp-value (below 0.01 or above 0.99) is strong evidence of a real discrepancy, and ppp-values should not be compared with significance thresholds as if they were classical p-values. The experiment below shows the effect.

### Bayesian residuals {#sec-pred-residuals}

For regression-type models, the **realised residual** $\varepsilon_i(\theta)=y_i-\mathbb E(y_i\mid\theta)$ is a function of the parameters and has a posterior distribution. Standardised versions divide by $\operatorname{sd}(y_i\mid\theta)$. Plotting posterior means (or intervals) of residuals against fitted values, covariates or time reveals misspecified mean or variance structures, just as in classical regression diagnostics. Unlike classical residuals, they carry parameter uncertainty automatically. A useful alternative compares $y_i$ with its predictive distribution through the probability integral transform, described next.

### Calibration and the probability integral transform {#sec-pred-calibration}

::: {#prp-pit}
## Probability integral transform
If $Y$ has a continuous distribution function $F$, then $F(Y)\sim\mathrm U(0,1)$.
:::

::: {.proof}
For $u\in(0,1)$ let $x_u=\inf\{x:F(x)\ge u\}$; by continuity $F(x_u)=u$. Then $\{F(Y)\ge u\}=\{Y\ge x_u\}$ up to a null set (on which $F$ is flat), so $\mathbb P(F(Y)\ge u)=1-F(x_u)=1-u$.
:::

A predictive distribution $F_i$ for observation $y_i$ is **calibrated** if the values $u_i=F_i(y_i)$ behave like independent uniforms [@dawid1982well]. A histogram of PIT values diagnoses the type of failure. A U-shape means predictions that are too narrow (overconfident), a hump means predictions that are too wide, and a slope means bias. For discrete data the randomised PIT $u_i=F_i(y_i^-)+V\,\mathbb P_i(Y=y_i)$ with $V\sim\mathrm U(0,1)$ is exactly uniform under a correct model. In-sample PIT values computed from the posterior predictive inherit the double use of the data and are slightly too concentrated, so for formal calibration assessment use held-out data or leave-one-out predictive distributions (@sec-model-comparison).

### Predictive accuracy and proper scoring rules {#sec-pred-scores}

A **scoring rule** $S(F,y)$ assigns a numerical score to a predictive distribution $F$ when $y$ is observed (here, lower is better). It is **proper** if the expected score under the true distribution $G$ is minimised by reporting $F=G$, and **strictly proper** if $G$ is the unique minimiser [@gneiting2007strictly]. Proper scores reward honest predictions. Two are used throughout the book:

- the **log score** $S(F,y)=-\log f(y)$, where $f$ is the predictive density or mass function;
- the **continuous ranked probability score** $\mathrm{CRPS}(F,y)=\int(F(z)-\mathbf 1\{y\le z\})^2dz=\mathbb E_F\lvert X-y\rvert-\tfrac12\mathbb E_F\lvert X-X'\rvert$, with $X,X'\stackrel{\text{iid}}\sim F$, which is computable from predictive draws.

::: {#prp-log-score-proper}
## The log score is strictly proper
For densities $f$ and $g$, $\mathbb E_{Y\sim g}[-\log f(Y)]\ge\mathbb E_{Y\sim g}[-\log g(Y)]$, with equality if and only if $f=g$ almost everywhere.
:::

::: {.proof}
The difference is $\mathbb E_g[\log(g/f)]=\mathrm{KL}(g\Vert f)$. By Jensen's inequality applied to the convex function $-\log$, $\mathrm{KL}(g\Vert f)=\mathbb E_g[-\log(f/g)]\ge-\log\mathbb E_g[f/g]=-\log\int_{\{g>0\}}f\ge-\log1=0$, with equality iff $f/g$ is almost surely constant on $\{g>0\}$ and $f$ puts no mass outside it, that is, $f=g$.
:::

The log score is local and severe: a single observation in a region where the predictive density is nearly zero produces a huge penalty. The CRPS is more forgiving and is expressed in the units of the data. The expected log score of a Bayesian model's predictions is the basis of the cross-validation criteria in @sec-model-comparison.

### What the posterior means under misspecification {#sec-pred-misspecification}

If the true data-generating distribution $g$ is not in the model $\{p(\cdot\mid\theta)\}$, the posterior still concentrates as $n$ grows, but around the parameter $\theta^\ast$ that minimises $\mathrm{KL}(g\Vert p(\cdot\mid\theta))$, and its spread need not reflect the true sampling variability of estimates of $\theta^\ast$ [@kleijn2012bernstein]. Intervals can be badly miscalibrated, as @exr-conj-7 showed for overdispersed counts, and the miscalibration does not disappear with more data. Model checking is therefore not optional.

## Worked example: annual counts of great discoveries {#sec-pred-worked}

The `discoveries` series gives the number of "great" inventions and scientific discoveries in each year from 1860 to 1959, as listed in the *World Almanac and Book of Facts* (1975 edition). It is a convenient count series. What counts as "great" is the almanac editors' judgement, so the data say as much about editorial selection as about the history of science.

```{r}
#| label: pred-data
y <- as.vector(discoveries); years <- 1860:1959
c(n = length(y), mean = mean(y), variance = var(y), zeros = sum(y == 0), max = max(y),
  lag1_autocorrelation = autocorrelation(y)[2])
```

**Model 1: Poisson.** $y_t\mid\lambda\stackrel{\text{iid}}\sim\mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda)$, $\lambda\sim\mathrm{Gamma}(2,0.5)$. The posterior is $\mathrm{Gamma}(2+\sum y_t,\ 0.5+100)$ (@prp-gamma-poisson). We draw $S=4000$ posterior values and, for each, a replicated series of 100 counts.

```{r}
#| label: pred-poisson-ppc
set.seed(801)
S <- 4000
post <- gamma_poisson_update(y, 2, 0.5)
lambda <- rgamma(S, post$a, post$b)
yrep_pois <- t(sapply(lambda, function(l) rpois(length(y), l)))     # S x 100
T_funs <- list(
  mean = mean,
  dispersion = function(z) var(z) / mean(z),
  zeros = function(z) sum(z == 0),
  max = max,
  lag1_acf = function(z) autocorrelation(z)[2],
  late_minus_early = function(z) mean(z[51:100]) - mean(z[1:50]))
ppc_table <- function(yrep) t(sapply(T_funs, function(f) {
  t_rep <- apply(yrep, 1, f); c(observed = f(y), rep_mean = mean(t_rep), ppp = ppc_pvalue(f(y), t_rep)) }))
round(ppc_table(yrep_pois), 3)
```

The mean is reproduced (ppp near $\tfrac12$), which is uninformative, as expected. The observed dispersion ratio is far above anything the Poisson model produces (ppp near 0), so the counts are overdispersed, and the maximum and the number of zeros point the same way: more extreme years than a Poisson model allows. The lag-1 autocorrelation is also far outside the replicated range: years with many discoveries cluster in time. The later half of the century has fewer recorded discoveries than the earlier half, more than in all but about 3% of replicates, which is mild evidence of a trend. The model fails in at least two distinct ways: overdispersion and temporal dependence.

```{r}
#| label: fig-pred-ppc-plots
#| fig-cap: "Posterior predictive checks for the Poisson model of the discoveries series. Left: replicated values of the variance-to-mean ratio (histogram) against the observed value (line). Right: the observed series (black) with five replicated series (coloured), showing the observed clustering and trend that replicates lack."
#| fig-height: 3.6
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
t_rep <- apply(yrep_pois, 1, T_funs$dispersion)
hist(t_rep, breaks = 40, col = course_fill, border = "white", xlim = range(c(t_rep, T_funs$dispersion(y))),
     main = "", xlab = "variance / mean")
abline(v = T_funs$dispersion(y), lwd = 2, col = course_ink)
plot(years, y, type = "l", lwd = 1.5, col = course_ink, xlab = "year", ylab = "discoveries", ylim = c(0, 13))
for (k in 1:5) lines(years, yrep_pois[k, ], col = alpha_col(course_cols[[k]], 0.6), lwd = 0.8)
```

**Model 2: negative binomial.** To allow overdispersion, let $y_t\mid\mu,\phi\sim\mathrm{NegBin}(\mu,\phi)$ with mean $\mu$ and variance $\mu+\mu^2/\phi$. This is equivalent to a Gamma–Poisson mixture with a separate rate for each year (@sec-prob-worked). Priors: $\mu\sim\mathrm{Gamma}(2,0.5)$ and $\log\phi\sim\mathrm N(\log5,1.5^2)$. There is no conjugate posterior, but with two parameters a grid on $(\log\mu,\log\phi)$ suffices. We sample grid cells with probability proportional to the posterior mass, then jitter uniformly within each cell.

```{r}
#| label: pred-negbin
lmu <- seq(log(2), log(5), length.out = 200); lphi <- seq(log(0.5), log(200), length.out = 300)
lp <- outer(lmu, lphi, Vectorize(function(a, b) {
  mu <- exp(a); phi <- exp(b)
  sum(dnbinom(y, size = phi, mu = mu, log = TRUE)) + dgamma(mu, 2, 0.5, log = TRUE) + a +   # + log-Jacobian of mu = e^a
    dnorm(b, log(5), 1.5, log = TRUE)                                                       # prior already on log phi
}))
w <- normalise_log_weights(as.vector(lp))
idx <- sample.int(length(w), S, replace = TRUE, prob = w)
h1 <- diff(lmu[1:2]); h2 <- diff(lphi[1:2])
mu_d <- exp(lmu[row(lp)[idx]] + runif(S, -h1 / 2, h1 / 2))
phi_d <- exp(lphi[col(lp)[idx]] + runif(S, -h2 / 2, h2 / 2))
c(mu_mean = mean(mu_d), phi_median = median(phi_d), phi_q05 = quantile(phi_d, 0.05, names = FALSE),
  phi_q95 = quantile(phi_d, 0.95, names = FALSE))
yrep_nb <- t(mapply(function(m, p) rnbinom(length(y), size = p, mu = m), mu_d, phi_d))
round(ppc_table(yrep_nb), 3)
```

The negative binomial reproduces the dispersion, the maximum and the number of zeros, but the autocorrelation check still fails. Both models treat years as exchangeable, and the data are not. A model with a time-varying rate (@sec-time-series) is needed for any question that depends on the time structure, such as forecasting the next decade.

**Predictive evaluation on held-out years.** We refit both models on 1860–1939 and score their predictions for 1940–1959 with the log score and the CRPS (lower is better):

```{r}
#| label: pred-holdout
train <- y[1:80]; test <- y[81:100]
pp <- gamma_poisson_update(train, 2, 0.5)
lam <- rgamma(S, pp$a, pp$b)
pois_pred <- sapply(test, function(k) log(mean(dpois(k, lam))))
lp_tr <- outer(lmu, lphi, Vectorize(function(a, b) sum(dnbinom(train, size = exp(b), mu = exp(a), log = TRUE)) +
  dgamma(exp(a), 2, 0.5, log = TRUE) + a + dnorm(b, log(5), 1.5, log = TRUE)))
wt <- normalise_log_weights(as.vector(lp_tr)); id <- sample.int(length(wt), S, TRUE, wt)
m_tr <- exp(lmu[row(lp_tr)[id]]); p_tr <- exp(lphi[col(lp_tr)[id]])
nb_pred <- sapply(test, function(k) log(mean(dnbinom(k, size = p_tr, mu = m_tr))))
draws_p <- rpois(S, lam); draws_nb <- rnbinom(S, size = p_tr, mu = m_tr)
rbind(log_score = c(poisson = -sum(pois_pred), negbin = -sum(nb_pred)),
      crps = c(poisson = sum(sapply(test, crps_sample, x = draws_p)),
               negbin = sum(sapply(test, crps_sample, x = draws_nb))))
```

The negative binomial gives the better log score, because its wider predictive distributions are not caught out by unusual years. The CRPS, which rewards sharpness more and is less sensitive to tails, separates the two models less. Neither score says the negative binomial is *correct*: the posterior predictive checks above showed that it is not.

## R implementation {#sec-pred-r}

The predictive tools are in `R/diagnostics/predictive.R`:

```{r}
#| file: R/diagnostics/predictive.R
```

A note on efficiency: replicated data sets are stored as an $S\times n$ matrix, so every test quantity is one `apply()` over rows. For large $n$ and $S$ this matrix can be big. Computing test quantities on the fly, one replicate at a time, avoids storing it.

## Computational experiment: how ppp-values behave {#sec-pred-experiment}

**ppp-values are conservative.** We simulate data from the model itself: the normal model with known $\sigma=1$, $n=20$, prior $\mu\sim\mathrm N(0,1)$. We compute ppp-values for two test quantities, the sample mean, which the model fits directly, and the sample maximum.

```{r}
#| label: fig-pred-ppp-distribution
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of posterior predictive p-values over 2000 data sets simulated from the model itself. For the sample mean (left) the ppp-value is concentrated near 1/2 and can never signal misfit; for the maximum (right) it is much closer to uniform. Both have mean 1/2."
#| fig-height: 3.4
set.seed(802)
ppp_sim <- replicate(2000, {
  mu <- rnorm(1); yy <- rnorm(20, mu, 1)
  po <- normal_known_var_update(yy, 1, 0, 1)
  mus <- rnorm(500, po$mean, sqrt(po$var))
  rep <- matrix(rnorm(500 * 20, mus, 1), 500)                         # row s uses mus[s]
  c(mean = ppc_pvalue(mean(yy), rowMeans(rep)), max = ppc_pvalue(max(yy), apply(rep, 1, max)))
})
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
for (nm in rownames(ppp_sim)) hist(ppp_sim[nm, ], breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.05), col = course_fill, border = "white",
                                   main = paste("T =", nm), xlab = "ppp-value")
rbind(mean = rowMeans(ppp_sim), P_below_0.05 = rowMeans(ppp_sim < 0.05))
```

Both distributions have mean $\tfrac12$ (@prp-ppp-mean), but the ppp-value for the mean never falls below 0.05, and the one for the maximum does so in fewer than 5% of data sets. A check is informative only when its test quantity is not tightly determined by the fitted parameters.

**PIT histograms diagnose the type of misfit.** For the discoveries data, randomised in-sample PIT values from the two models:

```{r}
#| label: fig-pred-pit
#| fig-cap: "Randomised PIT histograms for the discoveries counts under the Poisson model (left) and the negative-binomial model (right). The U-shape for the Poisson model shows predictive distributions that are too narrow."
#| fig-height: 3.2
set.seed(803)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
hist(pit_values(y, yrep_pois, discrete = TRUE),
     breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.1), col = course_fill, border = "white", main = "Poisson", xlab = "PIT")
hist(pit_values(y, yrep_nb, discrete = TRUE), breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.1), col = course_fill, border = "white",
     main = "negative binomial", xlab = "PIT")
```

## Diagnostics and validation {#sec-pred-validation}

- **Check the checking code** by applying it to data simulated from the fitted model. ppp-values should then be unremarkable, and their distribution over repeated simulations should average $\tfrac12$ (@prp-ppp-mean).
- **Use several test quantities**, each aimed at a specific assumption, and report all of them, not only those that pass.
- **Prefer held-out or cross-validated predictions** for calibration and accuracy assessments (@sec-model-comparison), since in-sample checks use the data twice.
- **Report Monte Carlo error** of ppp-values. With $S$ draws, the standard error of an estimated $p_B$ is at most $\sqrt{p_B(1-p_B)/S}$ for independent draws, and larger for MCMC draws.

## Interpretation {#sec-pred-interpretation}

The two models answer different questions. If we want the long-run average number of great discoveries per year, both give similar answers, and the negative binomial's interval is more honest. If we want to forecast the 1960s, neither is adequate, because both ignore the time structure that the checks revealed. Model checking does not produce a single verdict of "accept" or "reject". It tells us *which conclusions* a model can support.

## Limitations and common errors {#sec-pred-errors}

- **Double use of data.** The model is fitted and checked on the same data, so ppp-values are conservative and can miss real problems, especially for test quantities related to the fitted parameters.
- **Treating ppp-values as classical p-values** with a 0.05 threshold. They are not uniform under the model.
- **Testing what the model fits by construction** (sample means, totals) and concluding that the model is adequate.
- **Plug-in predictions** that ignore parameter uncertainty, which understate predictive variance (@eq-pred-variance).
- **Checking only the sampling model**, not the prior: prior–data conflict needs the prior predictive check of @sec-prior-conflict.
- **Assuming a model that passes checks is true.** Checks have limited power, and passing them means only that no discrepancy was detected in the directions examined.

## Chapter summary {#sec-pred-summary}

- The posterior predictive distribution averages the sampling model over the posterior. Its variance is sampling variability plus parameter uncertainty (@eq-pred-variance).
- Posterior predictive checks compare observed test quantities with their replicated distribution, and the ppp-value (@eq-ppp) summarises the comparison.
- ppp-values average $\frac12$ under the model (@prp-ppp-mean) but are typically more concentrated than uniform. Extreme values are informative, while moderate values are weak evidence of fit.
- PIT values diagnose calibration (@prp-pit). Proper scoring rules such as the log score (@prp-log-score-proper) and the CRPS measure predictive accuracy.
- Under misspecification the posterior concentrates on the KL-closest model, with possibly miscalibrated uncertainty, so model checking is essential.

## Exercises {#sec-pred-exercises}

::: {#exr-pred-1}
**[Mathematical ★]** For the Normal model with known variance (@prp-normal-known), verify @eq-pred-variance for the predictive distribution $\mathrm N(m_n,\sigma^2+v_n)$ and identify each term.
:::

::: {#exr-pred-2}
**[Conceptual ★★]** For each of the following, propose a test quantity aimed at the assumption in parentheses: (a) binary outcomes of 50 patients in 10 hospitals (no hospital effect); (b) daily rainfall (no zero inflation); (c) a linear regression of weight on height (constant variance); (d) reaction times (normality of errors).
:::

::: {#exr-pred-3}
**[Proof ★★]** Extend @prp-ppp-mean to discrete test quantities: show that $\mathbb E[p_B(y)]=\frac12+\frac12\mathbb P(T(y)=T(y^{\text{rep}}))$.
:::

::: {#exr-pred-4}
**[R ★★]** Apply the Poisson and negative-binomial posterior predictive checks of the worked example to the `InsectSprays` counts, treating each spray separately (six analyses). For which sprays is the Poisson model rejected by the dispersion check?
:::

::: {#exr-pred-5}
**[Mathematical ★★]** Show that the CRPS of a point forecast (a distribution concentrated at $x_0$) equals the absolute error $\lvert y-x_0\rvert$, so the CRPS generalises the mean absolute error to probabilistic forecasts.
:::

::: {#exr-pred-6}
**[Simulation ★★]** Repeat the ppp-value experiment for the test quantity $T(y)=\sum_i(y_i-\bar y)^2$ (the sample variance), with $\sigma$ known. Then repeat it when the data are generated with $\sigma=2$ while the model assumes $\sigma=1$. How often is the misspecification detected at $p_B<0.01$ for $n=20$ and $n=100$?
:::

::: {#exr-pred-7}
**[Critique ★★]** A paper fits a hierarchical model and reports: "Posterior predictive p-value for the chi-square discrepancy = 0.42, indicating excellent fit." What further information would you need before accepting this conclusion?
:::

::: {#exr-pred-8}
**[Research ★★★]** Calibrated alternatives to ppp-values include the *partial* posterior predictive p-value and simulation-based calibration of the ppp-value itself: compute $p_B$ for many data sets drawn from the prior predictive and report where the observed $p_B$ falls in that distribution. Implement the second approach for the dispersion check of the Poisson model of the discoveries data, and compare the calibrated p-value with the raw ppp-value.
:::

## Solutions {#sec-pred-solutions}

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution to @exr-pred-1
$\mathbb E[\operatorname{Var}(\tilde y\mid\mu)\mid y]=\sigma^2$ (sampling variability, constant), and $\operatorname{Var}[\mathbb E(\tilde y\mid\mu)\mid y]=\operatorname{Var}(\mu\mid y)=v_n$ (parameter uncertainty, $\approx\sigma^2/n$). Their sum is the predictive variance $\sigma^2+v_n$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution to @exr-pred-2
(a) The between-hospital variance of observed response proportions (or the maximum hospital proportion), which tests extra-binomial variation between hospitals. (b) The proportion of dry days. (c) The correlation between absolute residuals and fitted values, or the ratio of residual variances in the upper and lower halves of height. (d) Sample skewness and kurtosis of standardised residuals, or a QQ-plot discrepancy such as the largest absolute standardised residual.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution to @exr-pred-3
As in the proof, $\mathbb E[p_B]=\mathbb P(T^{\text{rep}}\ge T)$. By exchangeability $\mathbb P(T^{\text{rep}}>T)=\mathbb P(T>T^{\text{rep}})=:q$, and $2q+\mathbb P(T=T^{\text{rep}})=1$. Hence $\mathbb P(T^{\text{rep}}\ge T)=q+\mathbb P(T=T^{\text{rep}})=\frac12+\frac12\mathbb P(T=T^{\text{rep}})$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution to @exr-pred-4
For each spray, draw $\lambda\sim\mathrm{Gamma}(2+\sum y,0.2+12)$, simulate 12 replicate counts, and compute the variance-to-mean ratio. With 12 observations per spray the check has limited power. Spray F (observed ratio about 2.3) gives a small ppp-value, spray A (about 1.5) a borderline one, and C and E are consistent with the Poisson model. The pooled evidence across sprays is stronger than any single check, which motivates a hierarchical or negative-binomial model for all sprays together.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution to @exr-pred-5
If $F$ is a point mass at $x_0$, then $X=X'=x_0$ almost surely, so $\mathbb E\lvert X-X'\rvert=0$ and $\mathrm{CRPS}=\mathbb E\lvert X-y\rvert=\lvert x_0-y\rvert$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution to @exr-pred-6
Under the correct model, the ppp-value for the sample variance is close to uniform (the variance is not fitted when $\sigma$ is known), so $\mathbb P(p_B<0.01)\approx0.01$. When the true $\sigma=2$, the observed sum of squares is about four times its replicated value, and the misspecification is detected nearly always for $n=20$ and essentially always for $n=100$. When $\sigma$ is *also estimated*, the same check becomes useless, because the fitted $\sigma$ absorbs the discrepancy. This again illustrates that test quantities must not be fitted directly.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution to @exr-pred-7
A single moderate ppp-value is weak evidence of fit, because ppp-values are conservative and a chi-square discrepancy is closely tied to fitted variance parameters. One would want: checks aimed at specific assumptions (group-level normality, outliers, dependence); graphical comparisons of observed and replicated data; information on how many checks were performed and whether any failed; held-out predictive performance; and sensitivity of the conclusions to plausible model alternatives.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution to @exr-pred-8
Simulate $\lambda^\ast$ from the prior, data $y^\ast$ (100 Poisson counts) from $\lambda^\ast$, refit the conjugate posterior, and compute $p_B(y^\ast)$ for the dispersion check. Repeat 1000 times to estimate the null distribution of $p_B$. The calibrated p-value is the fraction of null $p_B$ values at or below the observed $p_B$. For the discoveries data the raw $p_B$ is essentially zero, and calibration does not change the conclusion. Calibration matters most for moderate raw values such as 0.1, where the null distribution of $p_B$ is concentrated near $\frac12$ and a value of 0.1 can be quite unusual.
:::
